```{r}
#| label: data-setup
#| code-fold: true

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(spdep)

base_path <- here::here("data")

survey_microdata <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "survey_microdata_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

la_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-ltla.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  select(la_code = LAD21CD) |>
  filter(str_starts(la_code, "W"))

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  select(
    area_id = MSOA21CD,
    msoa_name = MSOA21NM
  ) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W"))
```

```{r}
#| label: data-plot-config
#| echo: false
missing_fill <- "grey85"
legend_bar_width <- grid::unit(4.5, "cm")
legend_bar_height <- grid::unit(0.35, "cm")

count_map_theme <- theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
  )

chart_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title.position = "plot",
  plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 11)
)
```

## The Survey Microdata

The analysis uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on three waves of the **National Survey for Wales (NSW): 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025**.

The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.

The raw survey geography and stratification variable is Local Authority, while the estimation domain here is MSOA. The cleaned survey file therefore assigns each respondent to a synthetic MSOA within their Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. The resulting MSOA estimates should not be interpreted as substantive findings about individual places.

This design has two purposes:

- **Higher spatial resolution.** The synthetic MSOA assignment supports MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and unit-level SAE with poststratification.
- **Privacy and disclosure protection.** The assigned MSOA is not the respondent's true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations. 

::: {.callout-note}
Survey period labels use their end year. For example, the `2020-2021` survey wave is labelled as the `2021` wave.
:::

```{r}
#| label: data-geo-counts
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: "center"

la_response_counts <- survey_microdata |>
  filter(!is.na(strata)) |>
  count(strata, name = "responses")

msoa_response_counts <- survey_microdata |>
  filter(!is.na(area_id)) |>
  count(area_id, name = "responses")

la_count_map_data <- la_boundaries |>
  left_join(la_response_counts, by = c("la_code" = "strata"))

msoa_count_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(msoa_response_counts, by = c("area_id" = "area_id"))

plot_response_map <- function(map_data, title, border_colour = "transparent") {
  ggplot(map_data) +
    geom_sf(
      aes(fill = responses),
      colour = border_colour,
      linewidth = 0.15
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      direction = -1,
      labels = label_comma(),
      na.value = missing_fill,
      guide = guide_colourbar(
        barwidth = legend_bar_width,
        barheight = legend_bar_height
      )
    ) +
    labs(title = title, fill = "Responses") +
    count_map_theme
}

la_count_map <- plot_response_map(
  la_count_map_data,
  "Original responses by Local Authority",
  border_colour = "white"
)

msoa_count_map <- plot_response_map(
  msoa_count_map_data,
  "Synthetic responses by MSOA"
)

wrap_plots(la_count_map, msoa_count_map, ncol = 2)
```

## Data Preparation

### Target Estimand 

The *target estimand* is the quantity we want to estimate. It defines the outcome, population, geography, time period, and the auxiliary data needed for modelling, such as predictors or population counts.

> Estimate **what outcome among which population**, across **which geography** and **time period**.

For example,

{{< include assets/target-estimand.qmd >}}

The most common outcomes to estimate are **means** of continuous variables and **prevalence**—expressed as shares or proportions—within the target population.

### Estimation Domains

In spatio-temporal SAE, the estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination forms an area-time cell for which an estimate is required. The **estimation domains** are the complete set of these cells.

For the estimand defined above, the estimation domains therefore include every *MSOA-year* combination, including cells with no survey observations. For use in `INLA`, each area and time period is assigned a numeric index.

```{r}
#| label: data-inla-indices

area_frame <- msoa_boundaries |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(area_id, msoa_name) |>
  arrange(area_id)

area_index <- area_frame |>
  select(area_id) |>
  arrange(area_id) |>
  mutate(area_inla_id = row_number())

time_index <- survey_microdata |>
  distinct(time_id) |>
  arrange(time_id) |>
  mutate(time_inla_id = row_number())

domain_frame <- tidyr::crossing(area_index, time_index) |>
  left_join(area_frame, by = "area_id") |>
  select(area_id, time_id, area_inla_id, time_inla_id, msoa_name)

write_csv(domain_frame, file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"))

head(domain_frame)
```

### Survey Data

With the estimand being the prevalence of frequent cycling among the target population, we derive a binary indicator, `freq_cyclist`, from `AtFrqBke` (the active-travel question on cycling frequency).

| `freq_cyclist` | Coding rule | Meaning |
|:---:|---|---|
| `1` | `AtFrqBke` is `1` or `2` | Cycles at least several times a week |
| `0` | Any other valid `AtFrqBke` response | Cycles less frequently or never |
| `NA` | Missing or not asked |-W |

Each survey respondent may also require a design weight and other survey design components if available such as stratum, which are used to calculate design-based [direct estimates](direct-estimation.qmd), i.e. the estimated target population proportions or means using only the observed survey data. First, we include `strata`, which identifies each respondent’s sampling group and allows the variance calculation to reflect a stratified, non-random sampling design. Second, because the survey question was administered to the full sample in some waves and to a subsample in others, the appropriate `weight` variable varies by wave:

- Use `SampleTravelWeight` in survey waves where this question was asked to a subsample and the corresponding weight for this module exists (2023), 
- Use `SampleAdultWeight` in survey waves where this question was asked to the main sample (2021, 2025). 

The final survey indicator input has *one row per respondent-wave*:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `unit_id` | Unique identifier (respondent-wave) |
| `time_id` | Survey wave year |
| `area_id` | MSOA (Synthetic assignment) |
| `freq_cyclist` | Binary response |
| `strata` | Stratum |
| `weight` | Matched weight |

```{r}
#| label: data-survey-indicator

read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "surveyind_freqcyc.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(unit_id, time_id, area_id, strata, freq_cyclist, weight) |>
  head()
```

As an overview, the current cleaned data give the following usable observations for the cycling estimand:

| Year | Usable observations | MSOAs with usable observations |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2021 | 3,438 | 408 |
| 2023 (subsampled) | 1,989 | 405 |
| 2025 | 5,886 | 408 |

### Auxiliary Data for spatio-temporal SAE 

This tutorial assumes that all required forms of auxiliary data are available so that each method can be demonstrated. In practice, auxiliary-data availability, quality, coverage, and compatibility with the target estimand are important constraints on method selection.

| Auxiliary data | [Direct estimation](direct-estimation.qmd) | [Area-level SAE](area-sae-fh.qmd) | [Unit-level SAE w/ Summaries](unit-sae-summ.qmd) | [Unit-level SAE w/ Poststrat](unit-sae-mrp.qmd) |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Spatial graph |-| Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Modelling: Area-level predictors |-| Yes |-|-|
| Modelling: Unit-level predictors |-|-| Yes | Yes |
| Aggregation: predictor area summaries |-|-| Yes |-|
| Aggregation: poststratification table |-|-|-| Yes |

#### Spatial Adjacency Matrix

To represent spatial structure in the model, we construct an adjacency matrix identifying neighbouring MSOAs by their numeric indices. Neighbours are defined using Queen contiguity: two MSOAs are adjacent if their boundaries share an edge or a point. This structure allows the model to identify potential spatial autocorrelation and borrow information across neighbouring areas, supporting predictions for areas with limited or missing survey observations.

```{r}
#| label: data-inla-graph

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

# Write the Queen-contiguity graph in INLA's .adj format.
spatial_graph_file <- file.path(base_path, "clean", "msoa_queen.adj")
nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)
```
![](assets/spatial_weights_example.png)


#### Modelling input: Area-level Predictors

Area-level SAE models need area-level predictors that plausibly explain between-area differences in the target outcome. The area predictors are drawn from [ONS UK Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census) at MSOA level. These variables are chosen because frequent cycling is likely to vary with population composition, density, and car access.

The area-predictor input *has one row per MSOA*:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `area_id` | MSOA estimation area |
| `pop_density` | Population density |
| `age_adult_mean` | Mean adult age |
| `female_adult_share` | Adult female share |
| `caraccess_adult_share` | Adult share with car access |

```{r}
#| label: data-area-predictors

read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "areapred_freqcyc.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  head()
```

#### Modelling input: Unit-Level Predictors

Unit-level SAE models need predictors that can be used to model the outcome at the individual level. To model individual `freq_cyclist`, we extract or transform these unit-level predictors from the survey microdata *for each individual respondent row*:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `age` | Respondent age |
| `sex` | Respondent sex (`1` for Male, `2` for Female) |
| `caraccess` | Binary car access predictor (`1` for car/van available, `0` for none available) |

```{r}
#| label: data-unit-predictors

read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "surveyind_freqcyc.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(unit_id, time_id, area_id, sex, age, caraccess) |>
  head()
```

#### Aggregation input for unit-level SAE
##### Predictor area summaries {.unnumbered}

A unit-level SAE method can aggregate unit-level model predictions to target small areas using area summaries of the corresponding predictors. See [unit-level SAE with predictor summaries](unit-sae-summ.qmd)

E.g., 

|Predictor| Corresponding area summary |
|---|---|
|`age`, continuous|`age_adult_mean`|
|`sex_female`, binary|`female_adult_share`|
|`caraccess`, binary|`caraccess_adult_share`|

The previously prepared variables `age_adult_mean`, `female_adult_share`, and `caraccess_adult_share` can therefore serve two different purposes. In an area-level SAE model, they are used as area-level predictors. In a unit-level SAE model, they are used as area summaries of the corresponding unit-level predictors.

:::{.callout-note}
Area-level predictors only need to capture relevant variation between areas. Area summaries used to aggregate unit-level predictions must not only cover all unit-level predictors used in the model, they must also correctly represent the target population (e.g., the adult population) and therefore require a stricter preparation pipeline.
:::

#### Poststratification Table {.unnumbered}

A more sophisticated unit-level SAE method may use population cell counts, provided in a poststratification table, to aggregate fitted model predictions for each area-time cell. This weights predictions according to the target population distribution of the unit-level predictors instead of relying on area summaries. Predictors included in the poststratification table must be represented as categorical variables. See [unit-level SAE with poststratification](unit-sae-mrp.qmd)

We use a three-variable poststratification table with `age_band`, `sex`, and `caraccess`, sourced from [ONS UK Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census). The population counts must correspond to the target population defined by the estimand—for example, the adult population.

The poststratification output *has one row per area-time-age-sex-caraccess combination*:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `area_id` | MSOA estimation area |
| `time_id` | Survey year |
| `age_band` | Census age band |
| `sex` | Male / Female |
| `caraccess` | Binary car-access indicator |
| `pop_count` | *Adult* population count |

```{r}
#| label: data-poststrat-head

read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "poststrat_freqcyc_age_sex_car_21.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  head()
```
